title: Data acquisition tools for web data: how to choose one (with code)
summary: Web data acquisition tools come in five types. How to choose between buying and collecting data, plus a tested Python pipeline with real timings and costs.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:**


- "Data acquisition tools" covers two unrelated markets. **DAQ hardware** reads sensor signals in labs and factories. **Web data acquisition tools** pull external data from websites, APIs, and data providers.
- There are five ways to acquire web data. You can buy it, call an official API, query a search API, scrape and crawl pages, or drive a browser. Most pipelines combine two or three.
- Choose on cost per usable record, freshness, and upkeep. In our test, Firecrawl turned 10 catalog pages into **158 structured records in 16 seconds for 50 credits** , about a third of a credit per record.
- Mapping the same site returned **1,229 URLs in 1.1 seconds** for a single credit.
- Bought data is not automatically right. Firecrawl's company enrichment benchmark found employee counts averaged **57% accuracy** across six providers.


---


Search "data acquisition tools" and Google hands you oscilloscopes, USB measurement boxes, and LabVIEW. That's fine if you're logging thermocouple readings. It's less helpful if your manager wants competitor prices in a spreadsheet every Monday, or your AI agent needs product specs from 400 supplier sites.


External data acquisition is a different job with its own data collection tools. This post sorts the options and shows how to pick one. Then it walks through a working web data pipeline in Python, with the real output, timings, and credit costs from my runs.


## What are data acquisition tools?


Data acquisition tools are software or hardware that collect data from a source and turn it into something a computer can store and analyze. In engineering, that means DAQ systems reading analog sensor signals. In software and AI work, it means tools that pull external data from websites, APIs, and data providers into a database or an AI agent.


The two meanings share a name and almost nothing else:


DAQ hardware Web data acquisition


Source Sensors measuring voltage, temperature, pressure, vibration Web pages, PDFs, public APIs, licensed datasets


Typical tools DAQ cards, data loggers, LabVIEW, MATLAB Data Acquisition Toolbox Scraping and crawling APIs, search APIs, browser automation, data providers


Output Time series of sampled signals Records, Markdown, JSON


Hard part Sampling rate, noise, signal conditioning Page changes, JavaScript rendering, coverage, freshness


If you landed here looking for DAQ hardware or data acquisition software for sensors, a DAQ vendor's guide will serve you better. The rest of this post is about the web side.


## What types of web data acquisition tools are there?


Web data acquisition tools fall into five types. Data providers sell finished records, official APIs come from the site itself, and search APIs find sources. Scraping and crawling tools read pages, and browser automation clicks through pages a scraper can't read. The right type depends on whether someone already packages your data.


1. **Data providers and datasets.** Someone else collected the data and sells it per record or per file. Company firmographics, financial filings, and job postings are common examples.
2. **Official APIs.** The site publishes an endpoint for its own data. When one exists and covers your fields, it's usually the most stable route.
3. **Search APIs.** You start with a question, and a search API like Firecrawl[/search](https://www.firecrawl.dev/search) returns the pages worth reading, optionally with their full content.
4. **Scraping and crawling tools.** You have the URLs, or a site to walk, and need the content. This ranges from open-source libraries like Scrapy and Playwright to managed APIs like Firecrawl[/scrape](https://www.firecrawl.dev/scrape) and Firecrawl[/crawl](https://www.firecrawl.dev/crawl) .
5. **Browser automation and agents.** The data only appears after a click, a form, or a scroll. Firecrawl[/interact](https://www.firecrawl.dev/interact) drives a real browser for that, and Firecrawl[/agent](https://www.firecrawl.dev/agent) navigates sites on its own from a description of the data you want.


The five types differ most on freshness, upkeep, and cost model:


Type Freshness Setup effort Ongoing upkeep Cost model


Data provider Provider's refresh cycle Low Low Per record or per file


Official API Live Low to medium Low Free tier, then usage pricing


Search API Live Low Low Per query


Self-hosted scraper (Scrapy, Playwright) Live High High Your servers and engineering time


Managed scraping API (Firecrawl) Live Low Low to medium Per page, plus extras such as JSON extraction


Browser automation and agents Live Medium Medium Per browser minute or per task


## How do you choose a data acquisition tool?


Choose a data acquisition tool by working out the cost of one usable record. Add the tool's price to the engineering hours that keep it running, then divide by the records that arrive correct and on time. A cheap tool that needs weekly fixes often loses to a pricier one that doesn't.


These are the questions I'd answer before picking anything:


1. **Does a provider or API already sell this?** If yes, price it first. Collecting data someone sells cleanly is usually wasted effort.
2. **How fresh does it need to be?** Daily prices and weekly firmographics are different problems. Freshness sets your refresh schedule, and the schedule sets your bill.
3. **How many sources?** Five large sites and 5,000 small ones need different tools. Many small sites favor something that reads any page without per-site code.
4. **What shape do you need?** A spreadsheet row, a JSON object for an API, or Markdown for an LLM's context window. Converting formats later is extra code you'll maintain.
5. **Who fixes it when it breaks?** Count the hours. A scraper that breaks once a month on 50 sites is a part-time job.


On my test run, the managed route worked out to about 0.32 credits per record (50 credits for 158 records). That number is only useful next to the alternative's equivalent, so do the same sum for whatever you're comparing it with.


## Should you buy data from a provider or collect it yourself?


Buy data from a provider when it already sells your exact fields at the freshness you need. Collect it yourself when the data is niche, changes often, or lives on a few specific sites. Provider data also varies in quality, so test a sample against a source you trust before committing a budget.


In Firecrawl's[company enrichment benchmark](https://www.firecrawl.dev/benchmarks/company-enrichment) (October 2026), six providers filled in profiles for the same 200 US companies. Employee count was the hardest field, averaging 57% across the providers, with the best at 77.2% and the lowest at 46%. Two providers can sell the "same" field and disagree.


AI agents are spreading fast. In Stack Overflow's[May 2026 pulse survey](https://stackoverflow.blog/2026/05/27/agents-on-a-leash-agentic-ai-remains-mostly-monitored-at-work/) of 1,100 developers and working professionals, AI agent usage rose from 31% to 59% in a year. Cloudflare's[July 2026 report on the agentic internet](https://blog.cloudflare.com/agentic-internet-bot-report/) found that more than half of internet traffic is now non-human. An agent that needs company, price, or filing data needs a source it can call reliably.


The buy vs scrape decision doesn't have to cover the whole pipeline.[Firecrawl Alexandria](https://www.firecrawl.dev/alexandria) puts data providers and Firecrawl's own indexes behind the same API you use for scraping, so you can check whether a provider covers your data before writing a scraper. Discovery is free; running a provider's tool costs the credits it lists.

from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


firecrawl   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


result   =   firecrawl  .  search  (
"company headcount and funding data"  ,

If a tool fits, you call it with` firecrawl.scrape(alexandria={...})` and skip the scraper entirely. If nothing fits, you collect the data yourself, which is the rest of this post. The[Alexandria launch post](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/introducing-alexandria-series-b) covers how providers are paid when agents pull their data.


Collecting data yourself doesn't have to mean running scraping infrastructure.[Stanford AI Playground](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/customer-story-stanford) , which serves the Stanford University community, uses Firecrawl /search and Firecrawl /scrape for LLM grounding: it augments model responses with real-time web data from about 800 sources a day across more than 10,000 domains. Firecrawl is built for that kind of enterprise use, and 67% of Fortune 100 companies are Firecrawl users.

## How do you build a web data acquisition pipeline with Firecrawl?


A web data acquisition pipeline with Firecrawl checks Firecrawl Alexandria for ready-made data, finds sources with Firecrawl /search and lists a site's pages with Firecrawl /map. It then turns pages into structured records with Firecrawl /scrape and a JSON schema, scales that with Firecrawl batch scrape, reads PDFs with the same Firecrawl /scrape call, and watches for changes with Firecrawl /monitor. Each step ran against the live API on October 22, 2026.


The examples use Python, but Python is only one way in. Firecrawl has official SDKs for Python, Node.js and TypeScript, Go, Java, Ruby, Rust, .NET, PHP, and Elixir, plus a REST API you can call with cURL from anywhere. The[Firecrawl CLI](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/sdks/cli) runs the same calls from a terminal. The MCP server connects Firecrawl to AI assistants and coding agents such as Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and Codex. Agent frameworks such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, Mastra, CrewAI, and the Vercel AI SDK have integrations, and so do no-code tools like n8n, Zapier, Make, and Dify. The SDKs, CLI, and REST API share the same endpoints and credit pricing, while MCP and no-code integrations expose a subset of those endpoints that varies by tool.


The example tracks book prices on Books to Scrape (` books.toscrape.com` ), a sandbox store built for scraping practice, so you can run every snippet yourself without worrying about someone's production site.


### What do you need to install?


```text
pip   install   firecrawl-py
export   FIRECRAWL_API_KEY  =  fc-...
```


The snippets below read your key from` FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` . To try the Firecrawl /search and Firecrawl /scrape steps before signing up, create the client with` Firecrawl()` and no key, which uses Firecrawl's keyless mode (capped per IP address per day). Firecrawl /map, Firecrawl batch scrape, and Firecrawl /monitor need a key.


### How do you check Firecrawl Alexandria for ready-made data first?


Firecrawl Alexandria is the first stop in the pipeline because a provider may already return the records you planned to scrape. It works with the same API key as Firecrawl /scrape, so an agent can find a provider, read its inputs and price for free, then call it in one request. In Firecrawl's internal evaluations, AI agents using Alexandria scored 21% higher on answer quality than agents using built-in web tools, with the same model and prompts.


Here it pulls a company's annual reports straight from SEC EDGAR:


```text
import   os
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


firecrawl   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


filings   =   firecrawl  .  scrape  (
alexandria  =  {
"provider"  :   "sec-gov"  ,
"capability"  :   "filings/filings"  ,
"options"  : {  "ticker"  :   "AAPL"  ,   "forms"  : [  "10-K"  ],   "limit"  :   3  },
}
)
result   =   filings  .  alexandria  [  0  ]
print  (result.data[  "company"  ][  "name"  ],   "|"  , result.credits_cost,   "credits"  )
for   filing   in   result  .  data  [  "filings"  ]:
print  (filing[  "filing_date"  ], filing[  "form"  ], filing[  "primary_document_url"  ])
```


```text
Apple Inc. | 5 credits
2025-10-31 10-K https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019325000079/aapl-20250927.htm
2024-11-01 10-K https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019324000123/aapl-20240928.htm
2023-11-03 10-K https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019323000106/aapl-20230930.htm


```


Three annual reports, each with its filing date and a direct document link, came back as typed records for 5 credits. There was no page to parse and no selector to maintain.

A team building risk intelligence for enterprise AI agents with Firecrawl told us it would rather pull exactly what it needs through Alexandria than pay for bulk access to each source.


When a provider covers your data, stop there. When it doesn't, the rest of the pipeline collects it from the web.


### How do you find sources with Firecrawl /search?


If you don't know which sites carry your data yet, start with a query.


```text
import   os
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


firecrawl   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


results   =   firecrawl  .  search  (  "used book prices online store"  , limit  =  5  )
for   hit   in   results  .  web   or   []  :
print  (hit.url.  split  (  "?"  )[  0  ],   "|"  , hit.title)
```


```text
https://www.bookfinder.com/ | BookFinder.com: New & Used Books, Rare Books, Textbooks
https://www.betterworldbooks.com/ | Better World Books: Buy New & Used Books Online
https://bookoutlet.com/ | Book Outlet: Browse Discounted Books Online
https://m.alibris.com/ | Alibris - Buy new and used books, textbooks, music and movies
https://www.hpb.com/ | Used Books, Movies & Music


```


Results live under` results.web` , not` results.data` , which trips people up on their first try.


### How do you list every page on a site with Firecrawl /map?


Once you know the site, Firecrawl[/map](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map) returns its URLs without scraping them. It reads the sitemap and fills gaps from search results and earlier crawls.


```text
import   os  ,   time
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


firecrawl   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


start   =   time  .  time  ()
site   =   firecrawl  .  map  (url  =  "https://books.toscrape.com"  , limit  =  5000  )
print  (  f  "  {  len  (site.links)  }   URLs in   {  time.  time  ()   -   start  :.1f  }  s"  )
for   link   in   site  .  links  [:  3  ]:
print  (link.url)
```


```text
1229 URLs in 1.1s
https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/political-suicide-missteps-peccadilloes-bad-calls-backroom-hijinx-sordid-pasts-rotten-breaks-and-just-plain-dumb-mistakes-in-the-annals-of-american-politics_917/index.html
https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/pet-sematary_726/index.html
https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/vogue-colors-a-to-z-a-fashion-coloring-book_355/index.html


```


A Firecrawl /map call costs 1 credit no matter how many URLs come back, so it's the cheapest way to size a job before you commit to scraping it. My earlier[Firecrawl /map walkthrough](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/firecrawl-map-cheat-code-web-scraping) goes further on filtering the list.


### How do you turn pages into records with a JSON schema?


Pass a JSON schema and Firecrawl` /scrape` returns fields instead of HTML. There are no CSS selectors to maintain, so a layout change on the store doesn't break your parser.


```text
import   os
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


firecrawl   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


schema   =   {
"type"  :   "object"  ,
"properties"  :   {
"books"  :   {
"type"  :   "array"  ,
"items"  :   {
"type"  :   "object"  ,
"properties"  :   {
"title"  :   {  "type"  :   "string"  },
"price_gbp"  :   {  "type"  :   "number"  },
"in_stock"  :   {  "type"  :   "boolean"  },
},
"required"  :   [  "title"  ,   "price_gbp"  ]  ,
},
}
},
}


doc   =   firecrawl  .  scrape  (
"https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/category/books/travel_2/index.html"  ,
formats  =  [{  "type"  :   "json"  ,   "schema"  : schema}],
)
books   =   doc  .  json  [  "books"  ]
print  (  len  (books),   "books"  )
for   book   in   books  [:  3  ]:
print  (book)
```


```text
11 books
{'title': "It's Only the Himalayas", 'price_gbp': 45.17, 'in_stock': True}
{'title': 'Full Moon over Noah’s Ark: An Odyssey to Mount Ararat and Beyond', 'price_gbp': 49.43, 'in_stock': True}
{'title': 'See America: A Celebration of Our National Parks & Treasured Sites', 'price_gbp': 48.87, 'in_stock': True}


```


The travel category has 11 books, and all 11 came back. JSON extraction uses a model to read the page, so spot-check a sample against the page itself before you run an untested schema at volume.


### How do you scale up with Firecrawl batch scrape?


The same schema runs across many pages in one job. This version maps the category pages and scrapes the first 10 in a batch.


```text
import   os  ,   time
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


firecrawl   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


schema   =   {
"type"  :   "object"  ,
"properties"  :   {
"books"  :   {
"type"  :   "array"  ,
"items"  :   {
"type"  :   "object"  ,
"properties"  :   {
"title"  :   {  "type"  :   "string"  },
"price_gbp"  :   {  "type"  :   "number"  },
"in_stock"  :   {  "type"  :   "boolean"  },
},
"required"  :   [  "title"  ,   "price_gbp"  ]  ,
},
}
},
}


site   =   firecrawl  .  map  (url  =  "https://books.toscrape.com"  , search  =  "category"  , limit  =  100  )
categories   =   [
link  .  url   for   link   in   site  .  links
if   "/category/books/"   in   link  .  url   and   link  .  url  .  endswith  (  "index.html"  )
][  :  10  ]


start   =   time  .  time  ()
job   =   firecrawl  .  batch_scrape  (categories, formats  =  [{  "type"  :   "json"  ,   "schema"  : schema}])
elapsed   =   time  .  time  ()   -   start


rows   =   [book   for   doc   in   job  .  data   for   book   in   (doc  .  json   or   {}  )  .  get  (  "books"  , [])  ]
print  (  f  "  {  len  (job.data)  }   pages,   {  len  (rows)  }   books in   {  elapsed  :.0f  }  s,   {  job.credits_used  }   credits"  )
```


```text
10 pages, 158 books in 16s, 50 credits


```


Each page cost 5 credits: 1 for the Firecrawl /scrape call and 4 for JSON extraction. If you only need the text, drop the schema and ask for` "markdown"` , which costs 1 credit per page.


### How do you get data out of PDFs with Firecrawl?


A lot of the world's important information is buried in PDFs, including annual reports, regulatory filings, research papers, government statistics, and product spec sheets. None of it shows up in a page's HTML, so a pipeline that only reads web pages misses it, and any serious data acquisition plan needs a way to read them.


Firecrawl reads PDFs through the same Firecrawl /scrape call. Point it at a PDF URL and you get Markdown back, tables included. The engine underneath,[Fire-PDF](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/fire-pdf-launch) , is built in Rust and is one of the fastest PDF parsers in the world. It routes every page through[pdf-inspector](https://github.com/firecrawl/pdf-inspector) , Firecrawl's open-source Rust PDF library and a developer favorite with more than 19,000 GitHub stars. Text-based pages are extracted natively in milliseconds, and only scanned pages go to OCR.


In pdf-inspector's[published benchmark](https://github.com/firecrawl/pdf-inspector#benchmark) on 200 PDFs (refreshed July 31, 2026), it finished the full corpus in 0.47 seconds. LiteParse took 0.75 seconds, OpenDataLoader 2.6, and PyMuPDF4LLM and MarkItDown about 17 each. It also had the highest overall and table-structure scores.


```text
import   os  ,   time
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


firecrawl   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


start   =   time  .  time  ()
doc   =   firecrawl  .  scrape  (
"https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762"  ,
formats  =  [  "markdown"  ],
parsers  =  [{  "type"  :   "pdf"  ,   "mode"  :   "auto"  }],
)
elapsed   =   time  .  time  ()   -   start


print  (  f  "  {  doc.metadata.num_pages  }   pages in   {  elapsed  :.1f  }  s,   {  doc.metadata.credits_used  }   credits"  )
rows   =   [line   for   line   in   doc  .  markdown  .  splitlines  ()   if   line  .  startswith  (  "| "  )  ]
table   =   rows  [  rows  .  index  (  next  (r   for   r   in   rows   if   r.  startswith  (  "| Model"  ))):]
for   row   in   table  [:  6  ]:
print  (  "|"  .  join  (row.  split  (  "|"  )[:  4  ])   +   "|"  )
```


```text
15 pages in 0.4s, 15 credits
| Model | BLEU EN-DE | BLEU EN-FR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ByteNet \[18\] | 23.75 |  |
| Deep-Att + PosUnk \[39\] |  | 39.2 |
| GNMT + RL \[38\] | 24.6 | 39.92 |
| ConvS2S \[9\] | 25.16 | 40.46 |


```


The 15-page Transformer paper came back in under a second for 15 credits, 1 per page, and its results table arrived as a Markdown table with rows and columns intact. The` mode` setting is` auto` by default, which tries native extraction first and falls back to OCR per page.` fast` skips OCR, and` ocr` forces it for scanned documents. Add a JSON schema, as in the step above, to pull fields instead of Markdown. For a local file or a PDF that isn't public, upload it with[Firecrawl /parse](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/document-parsing) .


### How do you watch pages for changes with Firecrawl /monitor?


Prices change, so acquisition is rarely a one-off. Firecrawl[/monitor](https://www.firecrawl.dev/monitor) re-checks pages on a schedule and, with a plain-language goal, only alerts you when a change matches it.


```text
import   os
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


firecrawl   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


monitor   =   firecrawl  .  create_monitor  (
name  =  "Travel shelf prices"  ,
schedule  =  {  "text"  :   "daily"  ,   "timezone"  :   "UTC"  },
goal  =  "Alert when a book's price changes or a book goes out of stock"  ,
targets  =  [
{
"type"  :   "scrape"  ,
"urls"  : [  "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/category/books/travel_2/index.html"  ],
}
],
)
print  (monitor.id, monitor.status, monitor.schedule.cron, monitor.estimated_credits_per_month)


firecrawl  .  delete_monitor  (monitor.id)
```


```text
01a16527-9635-768b-adbc-5f11d00d21fa active 0 0 * * * 60


```


The daily check on one page came with an estimate of 60 credits a month, an upper bound that assumes every check finds a change worth judging. The last line deletes the monitor so the example doesn't keep running; leave it out for a real one. The[monitoring guide](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/monitor-website-changes-firecrawl) covers webhooks and whole-site monitors.


For pages that only show data after a click or a form, swap the Firecrawl /scrape step for Firecrawl[/interact](https://www.firecrawl.dev/interact) . For Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and other document files, Firecrawl[/parse](https://www.firecrawl.dev/parse) handles the conversion.


## What mistakes do teams make with data acquisition tools?


The most common data acquisition mistakes are choosing on sticker price instead of cost per usable record, scraping data a provider already sells, and skipping validation. Each one shows up months later as stale dashboards or an AI agent repeating bad numbers.


1. **Pricing only the tool.** A free library still costs the hours spent fixing it. Put engineering time into the comparison.
2. **Scraping what you could buy.** Check providers and official APIs first. Tool discovery through Firecrawl Alexandria is free.
3. **Trusting the first run.** A schema that works on one page can misread another. Spot-check a sample before a full run, and again after a site redesign.
4. **Ignoring freshness.** Data that was right last quarter can be wrong today. Set a refresh schedule or a monitor from day one.
5. **Collecting more than you need.** Every extra field is more storage, more validation, and more to keep current. Ask for the fields you'll use.
6. **Forgetting the site on the other end.** Hammering a small site with requests gets you blocked and hurts the people running it.
